sentence: Earth spins, so at the equator you're riding at about sixteen hundred seventy kilometers an hour.
claim: At the equator, Earth's rotation carries the surface at about 1,670 km/h (NASA Space Place gives 1,675 km/h).
note: Bible source (§7 #5): 1,675 km/h (1,041 mph). National Geographic (Equator, encyclopedic entry): about 1,670 km/h. Computed: 40,075 km / 23.93 h = 1,674 km/h. Less away from the equator (× cos latitude).

sentence: That's even faster than the speed of sound.
claim: Sound travels about 1,225 km/h in air at sea level and 15 °C, so 1,670 km/h is faster than sound.
source_title: Speed of Sound (NASA education sheet, grades 9–12)
note: Excerpt: sea level 340 m/s, 1225 km/h, 761 mph. 1,670 / 1,225 = 1.36 (Mach 1.4). The air moves with the ground, so no sonic boom (not said).

sentence: And Earth circles the Sun at about thirty kilometers every second.
claim: Earth's mean orbital speed is 29.78 km/s.

sentence: Since this began, you've covered over six hundred kilometers.
claim: At 29.78 km/s, Earth covers over 600 km in the roughly 21 seconds from the start of the film to this line.
note: Computed after voicing from the line's time in the film (see compile.py's assert): 29.78 × t ≥ 600 km. Relative to the Sun.

sentence: People once argued that if Earth moved, birds and clouds would be left behind.
claim: A traditional argument against a moving Earth (going back to Ptolemy's Almagest) was that objects not attached to it, such as clouds and birds, would be left behind.
source_title: Dialogue Concerning the Two Chief World Systems (Wikipedia)
note: The Dialogue's Second Day answers the classic objections to Earth's motion (falling bodies, birds, clouds). Ptolemy, Almagest I.7, gives the clouds-and-birds argument; an astronomer may prefer to cite it directly.

sentence: In sixteen thirty-two, Galileo answered with a ship's cabin.
claim: In his Dialogue Concerning the Two Chief World Systems (1632), Galileo described the cabin below decks of a large ship: flies, butterflies, fish in a bowl and dripping water behave the same whether the ship is at rest or moving smoothly.
note: Excerpt: in the main cabin below decks, flies, butterflies and other small flying animals, a bowl of fish and a dripping bottle behave identically if the ship moves uniformly; the motion is shared by everything, including the air.

sentence: Below deck on calm water, butterflies fly the same, moving or not.
claim: Galileo's cabin: the butterflies fly to every side alike whether the ship moves (uniformly, on calm water) or stands still.
note: Same passage as c6. 'Calm water' = uniform motion, no rocking.

sentence: You feel a change in speed, never the speed itself.
claim: Uniform motion in a straight line cannot be detected from inside; only acceleration (a change in speed or direction) can be felt (Galilean relativity).
note: Earth's spin and orbit are curved motions, so strictly they are accelerations, but far too small to feel: about 0.034 m/s² at the equator for the spin, 0.006 m/s² for the orbit (computed: v²/r).

sentence: Stillness is a feeling, not a fact.
claim: You cannot feel steady motion; feeling still says nothing about whether you are moving.

sentence: And the Sun carries us around the galaxy at two hundred thirty kilometers a second.
claim: The Sun (and the solar system with it) moves around the centre of the Milky Way at about 828,000 km/h (about 230 km/s).
note: Excerpt: about 515,000 mph (828,000 km/h). Computed: 828,000 / 3,600 = 230 km/s. Other estimates: Live Science 720,000 km/h. Bible §7 #5 [est.].

sentence: One lap: two hundred thirty million years.
claim: One orbit of the Sun around the galactic centre takes about 230 million years.
note: Excerpt: roughly 230 million years to complete one orbit. Chandra (NASA/CXC) gives the same; other estimates 225–250 million.

sentence: Last time we were here, the first dinosaurs were just appearing.
claim: The earliest known dinosaurs date to about 230 million years ago (Late Triassic, northwestern Argentina).
source_title: 150 Million Years of Dinosaur Evolution (American Museum of Natural History)
note: Excerpts: the oldest known bones are about 230 million years old (Science News, 'Dawn of the Dinosaurs'); the Natural History Museum (London): the first definitive dinosaurs around 230 million years ago. 'Last time we were here' = one galactic orbit ago (c9); 'here' is where the Sun was relative to the galactic centre, not the same stars (the galaxy's stars move too).

sentence: Light time, across what you've flown while watching: a twentieth of a second.
claim: At about 230 km/s, in the roughly 62 seconds before this line the Sun has moved about 14,000 km around the galaxy; light crosses that in about 0.05 s.
note: Computed after voicing (compile.py): 230 km/s × t / 299,792 km/s ≈ 1/20 s.

sentence: To the galaxy's center: twenty-seven thousand years.
claim: The Sun is about 27,000 light-years from the galactic centre (8,275 pc), so light from there takes about 27,000 years to reach us.
source_title: The Massive Black Hole (Max Planck Institute for Extraterrestrial Physics, citing GRAVITY Collaboration 2021)
note: The channel's one galactic-centre figure (episode 1, c12).
